near_miss.lead: Sea travel as wet paths: ὑγρὰ κέλευθα.
near_miss.why_not: The two exact formula occurrences are both Greek. The Norse anchor concerns combat and flight on foot, not sea paths. Searches of Old English wet/water and way forms and the wet-root index supplied no defensible second-branch cognate collocation; water imagery alone is insufficient.

near_miss.lead: A loved person as sweet light: sǿtasta ljós augna versus Homeric γλυκερὸν φάος.
near_miss.why_not: Search found Od. 16.23 and 17.41 addressing Telemachus as sweet light. The affective metaphor is close, but the sweet and light words are not cognate across this comparison; Greek also lacks the eyes genitive. Medieval biblical or general affective idiom remains a rival explanation. The Irish slab partner lacks the figure.

The Norse pivot concerns preparing a ship in spring and contains no glory-seeking phrase. External Vedic matches are recorded separately as a search lead; the anchoring rule prevents promoting those witnesses to slab anchors. Homer Il. 6.446 has fame as the object of winning, but its verb is different.

near_miss.lead: Rest by day and night: hvílði / quietus, nóttina / noctu.
near_miss.why_not: The rest and night vocabulary is cognate, but Norse reports a specific continuous day-and-night withdrawal before a decision whereas Plautus denies ever resting day or night. Corpus searches confirm ordinary nocturnal rest elsewhere; no distinctive shared construction beyond the natural day/night merism establishes inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Many severed heads likened to hail, grass and stars.
near_miss.why_not: The Irish recurrence is within one tradition. The Norse partner merely mounts a horse. Searches for stellar comparisons found Iliad 8.555-562, where many campfires resemble stars, not the Irish accumulated hail/grass/stars comparison; the nouns for stars are not cognate here. Generic multitude imagery is inadequate.

near_miss.lead: Natural pairs as oath guarantors: sun/moon, water/air, day/night, sea/land.
near_miss.why_not: Homeric searches found Earth and Sun as oath witnesses (Il. 19.258-260, also the sacrificial pair Il. 3.103-104). This supports a widespread motif, but not the same sequence or cognate phrasing; the slab Greek partner describes naval manoeuvres. No inherited wording demonstrated. Read usci as uisce water; the OCR Id in the day/night pair likely represents lá, but do not silently emend it for a claim.

near_miss.lead: Breaking law and peace versus dissolving treaties.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse speech links slíta lǫgin with slíta friðinn. Greek σπονδὰς λύετε and other Thucydidean search hits describe dissolving treaties, but neither verb nor object is cognate with the Norse wording. A readily renewed conceptual metaphor alone is insufficient.

near_miss.lead: Blessing of gods and non-gods, dee andee.
near_miss.why_not: Vedic searches found privative divine adjectives (e.g. RV 2.26.1 and 3.32.6), but no matching inclusive blessing of both classes. Greek atheist passages are likewise not the Irish inclusive merism. Irish andee is the negative counterpart of día, while the explanatory t-áes means the people/class. The Norse anchor supplies no matching phrase.

near_miss.lead: Father and mother coordination / parental merism.
near_miss.why_not: Irish coordinates a child’s parents; Norse strings successive ancestors; Atharvavedic plants have Sky as father and Earth as mother. Cognate kinship nouns occur, but their relations and contexts differ, and literal parent pairing is too predictable to establish a poetic inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Naming witnesses versus learning or making a name.
near_miss.why_not: Repeated Norse naming and summoning of witnesses is a legal formula, whereas Cambyses learns a city name and the Vedic son establishes a name for fame. Shared name vocabulary and awake/announce roots do not share syntactic roles or a congruent speech act.

search_lead.cognate: Old Russian славы (genitive singular of слава) and Vedic śrávaḥ (accusative singular of śrávas-) continue the klew- fame family; искати and ichámānaḥ/ichámānāḥ continue the h₂eys- seek/desire family, with related sk-present formation.
search_lead.argument: Both traditions make glory the goal/object of seeking, using two cognate lexical families. The Igor passage concerns warriors seeking personal renown; RV 1.126.1 praises a royal donor seeking fame, and RV 10.102.4 places the phrase in a competitive setting. This is stronger than merely co-occurring fame vocabulary, but differing case government and the late Slavic witness require caution. Vedic witnesses are outside this slab, so this is a search lead only.
